chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from the one who narrated it, from Abu Ja'far or Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A man was brought to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) who had confessed against himself of immorality. So the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said to his companions: 'Come to me tomorrow morning with your faces veiled.' So they came to him in the morning with their faces veiled. Then he said to them: 'Whoever has done the like of his deed, let him not stone him — let him leave.' He said: So some of them left, and some remained, and those who remained from among them stoned him.

key_terms.أَقَرَّ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ: He confessed against himself — voluntary self-incriminating admission, a valid basis for hadd in Islamic law
key_terms.الْفُجُورِ: Fujur — immoral/licentious conduct; in this legal context refers to sexual immorality (zina)
key_terms.فَلْيَنْصَرِفْ: Let him leave — a command to depart, disqualifying any would-be executioner who shares the sin
key_terms.مُتَلَثِّمِينَ: With faces veiled — wearing a lathama (face covering), used to preserve anonymity of the executioners
key_terms.يَرْجُمْهُ: Stone him — rajm, the hadd punishment for proven adultery/fornication under classical Islamic law

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali (AS) say about who may carry out the stoning punishment?
ai.summary: This hadith records an incident from the time of Imam Ali (AS) in which a man voluntarily confessed to a grave sin (fujur/immorality), triggering the hadd punishment of stoning. Imam Ali's instruction that participants veil their faces and that anyone who had committed the same sin must leave before throwing a stone reflects a foundational principle in Islamic criminal law: a sinner cannot execute punishment upon another for the same offense. The hadith illustrates the strict preconditions for carrying out hadd punishments and the moral weight placed on the executioners.
